Ensure that stop words constitute no more than 30% of the total words in your response.

message.content:
* The Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) hypothesis posits an inverted U-shaped relationship between per-capita income and CO2 emission intensities.
- Empirical validations by Grossman and Krueger (1991), Stern (2004), Panopoulou and Rafiq (2013) confirm nonlinear associations across heterogeneous country samples, though threshold income levels remain contested.

* Structural break analyses reveal temporal instability in emission-growth linkages, suggesting regime shifts driven by technological transitions, policy interventions, industrial composition changes.
- Breusch-Pagan, Bai-Perron breakpoint methodologies demonstrate that single-regression specifications mask substantial parameter heterogeneity across pre- and post-transition periods.

* Trade openness exhibits ambiguous effects on carbon intensities, depending on whether scale, composition, or technique effects dominate.
- Panel data evidence (Cole, Elliott, Zhang, 2017; Lo and Fang, 2016) indicates net-positive emission impacts in developing economies versus net-negative effects in advanced industrialized nations.

* Energy mix composition represents a critical mediating variable through which economic expansion translates into atmospheric carbon accumulation.
- Decomposition analyses (Ang, 2007; Wei and Lenzen, 2006) attribute differential emission trajectories to variations in fossil fuel dependency, renewable adoption rates, energy efficiency improvements.

* Institutional quality, regulatory stringency, environmental taxation frameworks significantly modulate the emission-growth nexus.
- Cross-country comparative studies (Acheampong, 2019; Wang and Shen, 2019) confirm robust governance mechanisms and carbon pricing instruments attenuate decoupling gaps between GDP expansion and emission reductions.

* Nonlinear and threshold modeling approaches have advanced beyond linear specifications, capturing asymmetric effects and state-dependent dynamics.
- Markov-switching models (Lee, 2005; Gil-Alana, 2009), nonlinear ARDL frameworks (Ponding, 2017; Dorko and Dago, 2019) document regime-dependent causal pathways between macroeconomic performance and environmental degradation.

* Spatial spillover effects and regional interdependence challenge traditional autarkic assumptions in emission modeling.
- Spatial econometric techniques (Anselin, 1988; Liu et al., 2020) reveal significant cross-border transmission of carbon footprints, necessitating integrated regional decarbonization strategies.

* Decoupling indices quantify the extent to which economic growth detaches from emission growth, providing policy-relevant metrics for sustainable development assessment.
- Absolute versus relative decoupling distinctions (Tapio, 2005; OECD, 2002) inform policy design, with absolute decoupling remaining empirically rare, primarily associated with post-industrial economies.
